articles/administration.html.title: Server administration | Uniform Chat
articles/administration.html.summary: Server administration If you are an admin of your homeserver, ⋮ → Server administration… manages it from the app. The menu item shows only for admins. It works with servers that have Synapse's admin API, as Uniform Chat Server does. Reports lists what users reported, newest first, with the reason and, for unencrypted messages, the message. Delete a report once you have dealt with it, suspend the reported user, or shut the room down. Accounts finds accounts by part of their user ID or name. Choose one to see its devices and where they last connected from, and to: Suspend it: the user can still read and leave rooms, but not send messages, join rooms or invite. Their app tells them. Lock it: the server refuses their devices until you unlock it; they stay signed in. Make admin, or take the rights away. Set a new password, which logs out their devices. Send a server notice, which arrives in their own Server notices room. Deactivate it for good. Registration tokens lists the tokens new accounts register with. Make one with a number of uses or days, copy it and share it; delete one to stop it working. Shutting a room down and deactivating an account cannot be undone, so the app asks first. You cannot suspend, lock, deactivate or take admin rights from your own account. Server notices Messages from your server's admins arrive in a room named Server notices, listed first and marked From your server. You cannot reply there.

articles/calls.html.title: Voice and video calls | Uniform Chat
articles/calls.html.summary: Voice and video calls You can voice call the other person of a direct chat. When your homeserver has a LiveKit server for calls, calls go through it, the way Element X and Element Call make them, so Element X users can answer and call you. Otherwise they go directly between the apps, the way Element on the desktop and Element Classic on Android make them. Both kinds of call ring here. Calling Open the direct chat, and press 📞 in its header. A bar at the top of the window shows the call: Calling… while it rings on the other side, then the call's length once you are connected. Answering An incoming call rings and shows the bar at the top, whichever room is open, with Answer and Decline. On Windows and Linux the app plays a ring tone of its own on the system's default speaker. When the app is in the background, a notification tells about the call. If you have the app on several devices, they all ring; answering on one stops the others. Video On a device with a camera, a phone or a Linux computer with a webcam, press 📹 in a direct chat's header to start a video call. When someone calls you with video, the bar says Incoming video call; Answer with video also sends your camera, and Answer answers with voice only. The app asks for the camera permission the first time. During a video call the video fills the screen; Chat shows the rooms and messages under a smaller call bar, and Video brings the full screen back. Your own camera shows small in a corner. Switch camera, shown when there is more than one camera, changes between them, e.g. the front and back cameras of a phone; and Camera off stops your camera until you press Camera on; the call goes on with voice. The picture turns upright when either phone is held sideways. A phone that cannot keep up with the other's video asks it for a smaller picture, 320x240 at 10 frames per second, and for full quality again once it can. The desktop app sends video from a webcam on Linux; your user needs access to it, usually as a member of the video group. On Windows it shows the other person's video, but cannot send video yet. During a call Mute stops sending your voice; the bar says muted. Speaker and Earpiece switch phones between the loudspeaker and the earpiece. Hang up ends the call, or cancels one that still rings. The bar says relayed when the call goes through your server's relay (TURN), e.g. when a firewall stands between you, and Reconnecting… while the network is down for a moment. After the call ends, the bar tells why for a few seconds. Phones The first call asks for the microphone permission, and on Android 13 and later also the permission for notifications. While a call goes on, a notification stays in the status bar, so that the call keeps going when you switch to another app. When there is no sound Try Test audio… in the settings: you hear yourself a second later. If you hear nothing there, choose the microphone and speaker in the system's sound settings.

articles/getting-started.html.title: Getting started | Uniform Chat
articles/getting-started.html.summary: Getting started The Uniform Chat app for Windows and Linux: rooms, messages, files and end-to-end encryption in a graphical window. In narrow windows it shows one pane at a time. Note The app is in early development. It covers everyday chatting and encryption; notifications on Windows are still to come. Requirements Windows 10 or later, or Linux An account on a Matrix homeserver, for example @alice:matrix.org Install See Installing: with apt on Debian and Ubuntu, from the release archives on Windows and other Linux systems, or from source. Sign in Enter your full user ID, such as @alice:matrix.org, and your password. The server is found from the user ID; give its address only when it has no discovery file, for example http://localhost:8008 for a server on your own computer. The app remembers the account, so the next start opens the chat without asking. ⋮ → Sign out logs the device out on the server and forgets the account. Create an account On the sign-in form, choose Create an account. Enter the user ID you want, such as @alice:example.org, where the part after : is the server, and a password of your own. Many servers do not let apps create accounts: then make the account on the server's website and sign in here. When the server needs more, the form asks for it on the first try: a registration token, which the server's admin gives to the people they invite; its policies, such as terms of service: open them from their links, then tick I have read and accept these policies. The app then creates the account and signs in to it. Delete the account ⋮ → Security and recovery…, then Delete account… at the end. Confirm with your password. You leave every room, your name and picture are removed, and every device is signed out. The account cannot be used again, and nobody can take its user ID. Next, see Rooms and Messages and files. Where things are kept What Where Messages, keys and files ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-desktop/ Remembered account and settings ~/.config/uniform-chat-desktop/settings.json On Windows, ~ is your user folder, for example C:\Users\alice.

articles/install.html.title: Installing | Uniform Chat
articles/install.html.summary: Installing The app runs on Windows 10 or later and on Linux, on x64 and arm64 processors. It brings everything it needs; no .NET or other runtime has to be installed. Apt install On Debian and Ubuntu, x64 and arm64, install from the apt repository of Uniform Chat, which is kept in its releases on GitHub. Add the repository once, with the key its packages are signed with: sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/apt/keyrings curl -fsSL https://github.com/tagcode/Uniform.Chat/releases/latest/download/uniform-chat-archive-keyring.gpg | sudo tee /etc/apt/keyrings/uniform-chat.gpg > /dev/null echo "deb [signed-by=/etc/apt/keyrings/uniform-chat.gpg] https://github.com/tagcode/Uniform.Chat/releases/ latest/download/" | sudo tee /etc/apt/sources.list.d/uniform-chat.list sudo apt update Then install the app, which also adds it to the application menu: sudo apt install uniform-chat Start it from the menu, or with the command uniform-chat. sudo apt upgrade updates it with the rest of the system. sudo apt remove uniform-chat removes it, but not your account and messages in ~/.local/share/uniform-chat-desktop. Windows Download uniform-chat-desktop-<version>-win-x64.zip (or win-arm64) from the releases and unpack it anywhere; the docs folder in it has this guide (open docs/index.html). Then run Uniform.Chat.exe. Windows may warn that the app is from an unknown publisher, because it is not signed yet; choose More info → Run anyway. Other Linux systems Download uniform-chat-desktop-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz (or linux-arm64) from the releases, unpack it and run the app: tar -xzf uniform-chat-desktop-*-linux-x64.tar.gz cd uniform-chat-desktop-*-linux-x64 ./Uniform.Chat You can also start it by double-clicking Uniform.Chat in the file manager. To add it to the application menu, run ./install-desktop-entry.sh in the same folder. Run it again if you move the folder, and ./install-desktop-entry.sh --uninstall removes the entry. From source With the .NET 10 SDK, from the repository root: dotnet run --project src/Uniform.Chat.Desktop

articles/messages.html.title: Messages and files | Uniform Chat
articles/messages.html.summary: Messages and files Messages Type in the box at the bottom and press Enter to send; Shift+Enter starts a new line. Markdown works: **bold**, *italic*, `code`, lists and quotes. /me waves sends an action. Messages from the same person within a few minutes are grouped under one name. Edited messages say (edited), and reactions are counted under the message. A deleted message shows as Message deleted for ten minutes; messages deleted before that are left out, so the room reads better. A message waits as Sending… until the server has it; it is kept on the device, so it is sent later even if the connection drops or the app closes. Without a network, the app still lists your rooms as they were when it was last connected, so you can read stored messages and write new ones, which are sent once the network is back. Scroll to the top to load older messages. Click a link to open it in your browser. Links to Matrix rooms and people (matrix.to) stay in the app: a room you are in opens, and other rooms and people go into the box above the room list, ready for Join or Chat. Right-click a message for a menu of its actions. On a phone, press and hold it: a sheet rises from the bottom with who sent it and when, a row of reactions, and the actions. Details… at the end of the menu shows the same sheet on the desktop. Back or a tap above the sheet closes it. Reply answers it; the reply shows a quote of the message. Esc or ✕ above the message box stops replying. React adds 👍, ❤️, 😂, 🎉, 😮 or 😢. Edit puts your own message back in the message box; Enter sends the new text. Copy image, on an image, copies the picture, to paste it into another app or another room. Copy text copies it. Copy link copies a matrix.to link to the message, for sharing with people in the room. Delete removes your own message for everyone. Report message and Report sender send a report, with the reason you pick, to the admins of your server; see below. Block sender hides the person's messages and invites. Reporting and blocking Report messages, people and rooms that break the rules: spam, harassment, sexual or violent content, or anything illegal. Reports go to the admins of your server, who can act on them; the person reported is not told. Report a message or its sender from the message's menu, and a room from the room's ⋮ menu with Report room…, or from its menu in the room list. Blocking someone hides their messages and invites from you, on all your devices; they are not told. Block from a message's menu with Block sender, or from the room's ⋮ menu with Block next to their name. Unblock there, or in ⋮ → Security and recovery… under Blocked users, shows their new messages again. Files 📎 next to the message box sends files. On the desktop you can also drag files onto the room, or paste copied files or an image, such as a screenshot, into the message box with Ctrl+V. On Android, paste a copied image or file into the message box: hold it and choose Paste. In encrypted rooms files are encrypted before upload. Images show a preview in the room; click it to open the image. Under a file or image, Open opens it in the app your system uses for its type, and Save… saves it where you choose. On Android, use Save…. Sharing from other apps On Android, Uniform Chat is in the share menu of other apps. Share a link from a browser, or a photo from the gallery, and choose Uniform Chat. The app opens and asks you to choose a room; Cancel stops sharing. Text and links go into the room's message box, where you can add to them before you press Send. Images and other files wait above the message box: Send sends them, Cancel drops them.

articles/notifications.html.title: Notifications | Uniform Chat
articles/notifications.html.summary: Notifications On Android and Linux, the app notifies you while it is in the background. ⋮ → Settings… chooses what notifies, each on its own: Setting Notifies of Default Incoming calls A call: the phone rings and vibrates, also on the lock screen; on Windows and Linux, a ring tone plays. Off, a call shows only in the open app. On Messages in direct chats Each new message in a one-to-one chat Off Messages that mention you A message that names you, in any room Off Invites An invite to a room or a chat On A newer message in the same chat replaces the previous notification. Windows does not show notifications yet. On Android 13 and later, the app asks for permission to notify once you have signed in. Allow it: without it, an incoming call rings, but nothing on screen tells which app rings or who calls, and messages don't notify. If you refused, ⋮ → Settings… says so under Notifications, and Allow notifications… opens the phone's settings for the app. The room list shows how many messages, and calls, you have not read in each room, and the window title counts the rooms with unread ones, such as Uniform Chat (2). Opening a room marks them read. In the background on Android To hear of new messages and calls while the app is off screen, the Android app needs one of these, chosen in ⋮ → Settings… → In the background: Own background connection, the default: the app keeps its own connection to your server. Android requires a notification for that, Keeps connected, swipe right to release; it is silent and sits with the silent notifications, and you can hide it in Android's settings of the app's Connection notifications. It works with any server and needs nothing else. Whether the app is online shows at the bottom of the room list, as Online or as what it is doing to connect. UnifiedPush: a distributor app such as ntfy keeps one connection for all your apps that use it, and wakes this app when there is something new. The app then needs no connection of its own and no notification for it, and uses less battery. Install the distributor first, then choose it here; Look for distributors again finds one installed while the settings were open. With UnifiedPush, your server sends the notice through the distributor's server, or the UnifiedPush project's public gateway when that server has no Matrix gateway of its own: only that there is a new event in a room, never what was written or by whom. The app wakes up and fetches the message from your server itself. A distributor's server also learns when you get messages, so prefer one you trust, or run your own ntfy. If the distributor is removed or stops, the app goes back to its own connection the next time it is opened.

articles/phones.html.title: Phones and narrow windows | Uniform Chat
articles/phones.html.summary: Phones and narrow windows On phones, and in windows narrower than 720 pixels, the room list and the room take the whole width in turn. Back, or ‹ in the room header, returns to the list.

articles/rooms.html.title: Rooms | Uniform Chat
articles/rooms.html.summary: Rooms The room list shows invites first, then favourites, other rooms and low-priority rooms. A number shows unread messages; it is highlighted when someone mentions you. Right-click a room in the list, or press and hold it on a phone, for its menu, without opening it. On a phone, a sheet shows the room's address, topic, members, encryption and ID above the actions; on the desktop, Details… at the end of the menu shows it. Mark as read clears the unread count. Favourite lists the room first, Low priority last; a room is one or the other, and Remove from favourites or Remove low priority puts it back among the others. Your other devices and Matrix apps sort it the same way. Copy link copies a matrix.to link to the room, for inviting people. Report room reports it to the admins of your server. Leave room leaves it. For an invite: Join or Decline. The box above the list does three things, and its button tells which: Type Button Does #room:server, !id:server or a room link Join Joins the room. @user:server Chat Starts a direct chat and invites the user. Anything else Create Creates a private room by that name. New private rooms and direct chats are end-to-end encrypted. The room opens once the server has it. Rooms of newer versions have IDs without a server, like !abc123. To join one by ID, give a server that is in the room after it, separated by a space: !abc123 matrix.org Links to such rooms carry their servers, and fill them in for you. An invite opens with Join and Decline buttons. The room's ⋮ menu sets the topic, invites people, lists the members, verifies them and leaves the room. Room directory 🔍 next to the box, or Room directory… in the ⋮ menu at the top, lists the public rooms of your server. Type in Search and press Enter to find rooms by name, topic or address. To browse another server, type its name in Server, such as matrix.org; leave it empty for your own. Join joins the room, which then opens.

articles/security.html.title: Security | Uniform Chat
articles/security.html.summary: Security Messages in encrypted rooms are encrypted on your device before they leave it, and only the devices of the people in the room can read them; the server only sees ciphertext. New private rooms and direct chats are encrypted from the start, and encryption cannot be turned off for a room again. The recovery key lets a new sign-in prove it is you and read messages from before it existed. Setting up recovery creates three things: cross-signing keys, which vouch for your devices; a backup of message keys on the server, encrypted so the server cannot read it; and the recovery key itself, which is shown once. Write it down or copy it somewhere safe. If you set up recovery in another app, such as Element, use that app's recovery key or passphrase. Verification compares seven emoji on two devices to prove that no one is in between. Both devices must show the same emoji in the same order; if they differ, cancel, and nothing is trusted. A device you verified receives the cross-signing and backup keys, so it does not need the recovery key. You can also verify other people, so you know their devices are really theirs. ⋮ → Security and recovery at the top of the room list shows this device's encryption keys and the account's state, and offers what is missing: Set up recovery, when the account has none yet. The server may ask for your password first. Unlock encrypted history: messages sent before this device signed in are encrypted with keys the device does not have. Enter the recovery key or passphrase, from this app or another one such as Element, and choose Recover. The app restores the keys from the backup, shows the messages, and verifies this device. Verify with another device where you are signed in: accept the request there, and when both show the same emoji, choose They match on both. When another device asks to verify this one, the app shows the request; choose Accept and compare the emoji the same way. Below that, Devices lists where you are signed in. Verify asks a device that is not verified yet to compare emoji, and Sign out… signs a lost or old device out after you enter your password. To verify another person, open the room's ⋮ menu and choose Verify next to their name. They accept on their device, and you both compare the emoji. In your direct chat with them, the request is a message in the chat, as Element sends it, and Element shows it there too; elsewhere it goes to their devices. When someone asks to verify you from their app, the request shows in your direct chat and the app asks you to accept it. At the end, Blocked users lists the people you have blocked, with Unblock, and Delete account… deletes your account, as Getting started tells.

articles/settings.html.title: Settings | Uniform Chat
articles/settings.html.summary: Settings ⋮ → Settings at the top of the room list sets the theme (follow the system, light or dark), the text size (very small to very large, for the whole window: titles, messages and the message field), and which notifications to show; see Notifications. Changes are saved right away. Audio test Test audio… in the settings plays your microphone back a second later, through the Opus codec that calls use, to try the microphone and the speaker before a call. Choose Start, speak, and listen; Stop shows how long it recorded and at what bit rate. Silence means the input is not a microphone: choose one in the system's sound settings. On phones, the switch chooses the loudspeaker or the earpiece; with the earpiece, hold the phone to your ear. The first start asks for permission to record audio. Logs Logs… in the settings shows what the app has logged: the session's connection, sync, encryption and calls, as in the terminal client's log window. The list at the top chooses the session, the newest marked (now); the level chooses how much detail; the filter shows only entries with the text. Newest entries come first. Refresh reads the log again, and Copy copies the shown entries, e.g. to send with a bug report. The logs stay on the device. Licences The bottom of the settings shows the app's version, such as Uniform Chat 0.1.36 (6078a19), with the code it was built from in brackets. Mention it when you report a problem. Licences… at the bottom of the settings shows the license of Uniform Chat and of everything the app includes: the .NET runtime and each library, with its copyright notice. Choose one in the list to read it; ‹ goes back to the settings, as does the back button on Android.

index.html.title: Desktop Client | Uniform Chat
index.html.summary: Uniform Chat A chat app for Matrix, the open chat protocol, for Windows and Linux: rooms, formatted messages, replies and reactions, files, invites, and end-to-end encryption with recovery and emoji verification. Messages you write are kept on the device until the server has them, so nothing is lost when the connection drops. Note The app is in early development. Installing: with apt on Debian and Ubuntu, on Windows and on other Linux systems. Getting started: sign in, and where your data is kept. Rooms: the room list, joining and creating rooms. Messages and files: writing, replies, reactions and files. Security: encryption, recovery key and verification. Notifications: when and how the app tells you about messages. Settings: what can be changed. Phones and narrow windows: the one-pane layout. The same app runs on Android; see the Android guide. There is also a client for the text terminal; see its guide. To run a homeserver of your own, see the server guide.
